extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, metric-reform advocates, scientists, linguists, and the general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and recommended principles for modifying the metric system (nomenclature, denominations, and notation) to increase popular adoption and usability, with illustrative examples and suggested transitions. Also includes detailed technical specifications and operational notes for Pictet's gas-liquefaction apparatus (experimental reproduction guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandon present metric nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire abandonment of the present elaborate and ingenious system of nomenclature, and of any attempt at universality in the words employed to designate the units of the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: metric names are learned, unnatural to common people, hard to pronounce and remember; they impede adoption. Anti-pattern: insisting on Latin/Greek-derived metric names (millimetre, kilodollar-style) for universal spoken use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express units in each nation's vernacular
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression of each unit by each nation in its own vernacular tongue — the units themselves being the same everywhere, but the expression in language adapted to the familiar tongue of each people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: keep the universal magnitudes but allow local spoken names that are familiar and mnemonic. Example: retain 'dollar' but apply metric scaling (if desired) with vernacular names rather than introducing foreign-sounding terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use common notation as the means of universality
rubrics_metrics.description: A common notation as the means of universality, instead of a common system of names — the units and their written expression being thus universally the same, while the spoken expression conforms to national usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestion: devise universal visual symbols (line for length, square for surface, cube for solid, cup for capacity, coin for money, two lines for angle, waving line for time). Notation addresses the eye; spoken names can vary by language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names should be suggestive of familiar objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The words selected to express the several units to be suggestive of easy standards of comparison with familiar objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: hair's-breadth, pin, nail, hand (decimetre), long yard (metre), stone's-throw (100 m), short mile/kile (1,000 m). Rationale: concrete familiar referents aid memorability and daily use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation should be visually suggestive
rubrics_metrics.description: The notation also to be suggestive to the eye, as the nomenclature heretofore in use was to the learned ear, but not to the unlearned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design notation that communicates unit type and scale at a glance. The page suggests simple pictorial base symbols (line, square, cube, cup, coin, etc.) and a clear, self-explanatory visual system for scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce number of denominations
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of denominations to be reduced in conformity with an observed tendency among men to use numbers instead; oral expression to be simplified; and a suitable actual system of notation suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical principle: people practically use only two denominations (e.g., dollars and cents). Recommendation: limit denominations per table to two well-chosen units where practical, or otherwise greatly reduce counts to simplify use and mental calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition must minimize loss of familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition to the new system to involve the least practicable loss of familiarity — either with familiar objects or familiar names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation guidance: preserve familiar names or objects where possible to ease adoption (e.g., adapt existing names like 'yard' or 'dollar'). Phased change and notation continuity help public acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for directness and simplicity; adapt to human habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications of the metric system are needed to fit it for common use: roughly, directness and simplicity; adapt the system to human experience and habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: scientific correctness alone is insufficient; systems must be designed for untechnical everyday users. Anti-pattern: imposing complex learned nomenclature that meets scientific elegance but fails in popular adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer independent, concrete unit names over derivational prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Each and every unit in each table should have its own strong, independent name, instead of a name referring to the base-unit (avoid naming every unit as a prefixed form of a base-unit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: independence of names avoids confusing similarity (decigram, decimeter, deci-arc all sounding alike). Suggestion: choose distinct names so each unit 'stands alone' and is easily recognized without needing to recall a decimal prefix system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uniform-sounding metric prefixes across different measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sameness of words (uniform prefixes) in the metrical household, which makes units hard to distinguish; metric names often 'all look and jabber alike' to the unlearned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: deci-, centi-, kilo- applied across many measures produces near-homogeneous vocabulary that is difficult to parse in everyday speech. Remedy: use distinct names or vernacular variants to break monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make unit names answer natural questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit names should simply answer the natural questions: 'How long is it? How big (square)? How heavy?' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical naming principle: names should convey scale or referent (e.g., 'nail' for small length, 'yard' for medium), enabling intuitive understanding without technical training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow flexible cental/decimal scaling and pragmatic denomination choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not insist dogmatically on one exact scale for all contexts (strict decimal for every 10, cental for every 100, or eclectic varying with subject-matter); choose scale and denominations pragmatically per use-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: the cental scale may suffice for many uses (ten cents vice a dime); practical acceptance matters. The author declines to fix exact denominations but advocates reduction and adaptation to human usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use common, short, familiar roots where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer existing familiar names or short new vernacular terms rather than long learned words; 'new words are harder than new things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: French retained units but rejected new names; the essay stresses the vitality of old words and recommends stretching a familiar name to cover a new unit rather than inventing foreign-sounding terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide simple illustrative tables anchored to familiar referents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design unit tables that are anchored to everyday referents (e.g., 100 hairs = 1 nail; 100 nails = 1 yard; 1,000 yards = 1 kile), making the scale concrete and memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These illustrative tables are not final prescriptions but show how to choose units that readily map to ordinary experience; microscopic and astronomical extensions may be added as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notation and symbols to enable universality even if spoken names vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal written symbols/notation can preserve universality of the system while allowing local spoken vocabularies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation: adopt a standardized set of written marks or pictograms for base-unit types and scales, so international calculations remain unambiguous even when people use different vernacular names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pumps must be coupled to maximize pressure difference for liquefaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use compound exhausting and forcing pumps (paired and coupled) so as to produce the widest possible difference between the pressures of exhaustion and compression when attempting gas liquefaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational detail from Pictet's apparatus: two compound pumps acting on a refrigerant (sulphurous acid or carbonic acid) are coupled in this manner; coupling and pump design are critical to reaching requisite low temperatures and high compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain refrigerant conditions for staged cooling (sulphurous acid and carbonic acid specs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain anhydrous sulphurous acid in a receiver at pressure/temperature such that it evaporates at −65°C; condense and liquefy it at about −25°C and ~2.5 atmospheres; use carbonic acid at conditions evaporating at −140°C and liquefied under ~5 atmospheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: sulphurous acid circulated between receiver and condenser to provide intermediate cooling; carbonic acid reservoir surrounded by sulphurous acid reservoir to achieve very low temperatures necessary for liquefying gases like oxygen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retort and containment must withstand very high pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a wrought-iron retort (or similar) of sufficient thickness to withstand pressures up to ~500 atmospheres for oxygen liberation and compression; tubes and manometers must be rated accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example specs: retort to hold chlorate of potash heated to liberate oxygen; connecting glass or iron tubes (one described: 5 metres, 214 mm internal diameter) closed at both ends with cock for controlled release; Bourdon manometer graduated to 800 atmospheres recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immerse compression tubes in liquid refrigerant and monitor pressure-temperature behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Compress and condense gas in a closed tube completely immersed in liquid carbonic acid (or equivalent refrigerant) to induce liquefaction; monitor pressure changes (manometer) as evidence of phase transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational evidence: manometer rise to ~560 atm then fall to ~505 atm indicates portion of gas transitioning to liquid at −140°C. Sudden opening of orifice yields violent jet containing liquid/solid globules; electric light can enhance observation of phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drive apparatus with sufficiently powerful and stable motive force
rubrics_metrics.description: Operate pumps with an adequately rated engine (example: 15-horsepower steam-engine used in experiments) to achieve prolonged pumping and stable pressure differentials necessary for liquefaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pumps run for several hours to reach equilibrium temperatures and pressures (reported example: after several hours, tube pressure reached ~320 atmospheres at −140°C before final compression to 560 atm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate condensers and heat-exchange arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensers cooled by cold water (for sulphurous acid) and arrangement of reservoirs (carbonic-acid condenser surrounded by sulphurous-acid receiver) are necessary to stepwise accomplish the cooling and liquefaction chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the condensers and circulation tubes so liquefied refrigerant returns to receivers through small tubes as fast as liquefied; ensure insulating casings (wooden cases packed with poor conductors) and proper packing to limit heat ingress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental observation and instrumentation for phase identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use visual observation (e.g., electric light directed onto escaping jet) and pressure readings to identify presence of liquid/solid phases in escaping gas jets, noting color differences (white central cone indicating liquid/solid elements; blue external showing gaseous return).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine manometer readings with optical observation to confirm partial liquefaction; collect liquefied gas in receiver if feasible.
